claims.text: Conventional automotive exhaust catalysts use high platinum-group-metal loadings on standard alumina-based supports.
Incorporating ceria nanoparticles into an alumina-based catalyst support improves platinum-group-metal dispersion.
Improved platinum-group-metal dispersion enhances catalytic activity in automotive exhaust catalysts.
Improved platinum-group-metal dispersion enhances catalyst durability.
Ceria incorporation can preserve activity and durability while reducing precious-metal loading.
Ceria-doped alumina produces enhanced metal-support interactions at platinum–support interfaces.
Enhanced platinum–ceria/support interactions improve platinum dispersion.
Enhanced platinum–ceria/support interactions stabilize active sites.
Ceria provides additional oxygen-storage capacity.
Ceria more strongly anchors platinum particles.
Stronger anchoring of platinum particles minimizes sintering.
Ceria improves redox cycling relevant to automotive exhaust catalysis.
The combination of oxygen storage, platinum anchoring, reduced sintering, and improved redox cycling permits lower platinum use without loss of performance.
Ceria-doped catalysts at reduced platinum loading will have higher catalytic conversion rates than conventional catalysts.
Ceria-doped catalysts at reduced platinum loading will retain activity for longer than conventional catalysts.
The proposed improvement depends on homogeneous ceria dispersion.
The proposed improvement depends on ceria participating effectively in oxygen storage.
The benefits may diminish when operating conditions do not activate ceria's oxygen-storage mechanism.
The benefits may diminish when synthesis parameters are not optimized.
Direct experimental evidence under full-scale automotive exhaust conditions is currently lacking.

contradictions.description: The stated baseline is an undoped-alumina catalyst with high platinum-group-metal loading, but the experiment reduces platinum loading in both groups and the falsification rule compares the groups at reduced loadings. Thus, the decisive experimental control does not clearly match the stated high-loading baseline.
